nodes.title: Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Protocol
nodes.summary: This protocol covers antimicrobial prophylaxis for various surgeries, detailing optimal timing, single-dose principles, and agent selection based on procedure type and allergies. It also addresses special populations, MRSA colonization, and required documentation for compliance auditing.

children.title: Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Protocol — Overview
children.summary: This document is a synthetic test document for an indexing pipeline and provides no clinical guidance. It contains plausible but unusable recommendations regarding Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Protocol.
children.content:
> **SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT — NOT CLINICAL GUIDANCE.** Written to exercise the
> ingest, indexing and retrieval pipeline. The recommendations below are
> plausible in shape but must never be used for patient care.

children.title: Scope
children.summary: This protocol details antimicrobial prophylaxis for adults undergoing elective and emergency surgery in operating theaters. It explicitly excludes treatment for established infections.
children.content:
This protocol covers antimicrobial prophylaxis for adults undergoing elective and
emergency surgery in theatres. It does not cover treatment of established
infection, for which the antimicrobial stewardship policy applies.

children.title: Timing
children.summary: The passage details optimal timing for surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis, specifying a 60-minute window before incision for peak tissue concentrations. It notes that Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones require a 120-minute infusion starting at induction or earlier.
children.content:
The single most important determinant of efficacy is timing. Administer the
prophylactic dose within 60 minutes before knife-to-skin, so that tissue
concentrations are at their peak when the incision is made.

Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones require a 120-minute window because they must be
infused slowly. Start these at induction or earlier, and never rush the infusion
to meet the incision time.

A dose given after the incision provides no benefit and should be documented as
a protocol deviation.

children.title: Single Dose Principle
children.summary: This section details the Single Dose Principle for prophylaxis, advising against extending antibiotics past wound closure. It also covers guidelines for intraoperative redosing based on procedure length or blood loss, and when to discontinue prophylaxis due to drains or catheters.

children.title: Single Dose Principle — Overview
children.summary: The passage defines prophylaxis as a single dose and warns that extending antimicrobial prophylaxis past wound closure does not reduce surgical site infection while increasing Clostridioides difficile infection, resistance, and cost.
children.content:
Prophylaxis means one dose. Prolonging prophylaxis beyond wound closure does not
reduce surgical site infection and does increase Clostridioides difficile
infection, resistance and cost.

children.title: Intraoperative Redosing
children.summary: Intraoperative redosing guidelines specify when to repeat antimicrobial doses based on procedure length (exceeding two half-lives) or blood loss (>1500 mL). Specific examples include cefazolin and cefuroxime requiring redosing at 4 hours, while metronidazole does not.
children.content:
Redose intraoperatively when the procedure exceeds two half-lives of the agent,
or when blood loss exceeds 1500 mL. For cefazolin this means redosing at 4 hours;
for cefuroxime at 4 hours; for metronidazole no redose is required.

Redosing is not an extension of prophylaxis — it maintains the concentration of
the single perioperative exposure.

children.title: Drains and Catheters
children.summary: The passage advises against continuing antimicrobial prophylaxis when a drain, catheter, or line remains in place because evidence does not support its prevention of device-related infection, leading to unnecessary antibiotic use.
children.content:
Do not continue prophylaxis because a drain, catheter or line remains in place.
There is no evidence that it prevents device-related infection, and the practice
is a common source of unnecessary antibiotic days.

children.title: Agent Selection by Procedure
children.summary: This section outlines antimicrobial prophylaxis guidelines based on surgical cleanliness and specific patient allergies. It details agents for clean procedures, regimens for clean-contaminated surgeries, and management strategies for penicillin allergy.

children.title: Clean Procedures
children.summary: The passage specifies cefazolin 2 g IV as the standard prophylactic agent for clean orthopaedic, vascular, and cardiac surgery, increasing to 3 g for patients over 120 kg. It also notes prophylaxis is not needed for simple procedures without prosthetic material.
children.content:
For clean orthopaedic, vascular and cardiac surgery, cefazolin 2 g intravenously
is the standard agent, increased to 3 g for patients weighing 120 kg or more.

Prophylaxis is not indicated for clean procedures without prosthetic material,
such as simple hernia repair without mesh or excision of a skin lesion.

children.title: Clean-Contaminated Procedures
children.summary: This passage details antimicrobial prophylaxis regimens for different types of surgery. It specifies cefuroxime plus metronidazole for colorectal procedures and cefuroxime alone for biliary, gastroduodenal, and gynaecological surgeries.
children.content:
Colorectal surgery requires cover for Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms:
cefuroxime 1.5 g plus metronidazole 500 mg intravenously. Oral neomycin and
erythromycin with mechanical bowel preparation may be added where local policy
supports it.

Biliary, gastroduodenal and gynaecological surgery are covered by cefuroxime 1.5
g alone.

children.title: Penicillin Allergy
children.summary: The passage discusses penicillin allergy management, noting that a rash alone is not a contraindication for cephalosporins due to low cross-reactivity (<2%). For severe allergies, it recommends teicoplanin plus gentamicin, with metronidazole added for anaerobic coverage.
children.content:
Establish the nature of the reported reaction. A rash without features of
anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to a cephalosporin: the cross-reactivity
rate is under 2%, and substituting vancomycin unnecessarily is associated with
higher surgical site infection rates.

For genuine severe allergy, use teicoplanin plus gentamicin for clean procedures,
adding metronidazole where anaerobic cover is required.

children.title: Special Populations
children.summary: This section covers antimicrobial prophylaxis adjustments for special populations, including guidelines for renal impairment dosing and specific recommendations for administering prophylactic antibiotics to elderly and frail patients.

children.title: Renal Impairment
children.summary: The passage discusses prophylactic dosing for renal impairment, noting that most doses are single and require no adjustment. It specifically advises using a single 3 mg/kg dose of Gentamicin and avoiding it if the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 20 mL/min.
children.content:
Prophylactic doses are single doses and generally need no adjustment for renal
function. Gentamicin is the exception: use a single 3 mg/kg dose and avoid it
altogether where the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 20 mL/min.

children.title: Elderly and Frail Patients
children.summary: This passage advises on antimicrobial prophylaxis for elderly and frail patients, emphasizing weight-based dosing due to overestimated lean body mass. It specifically cautions about adding gentamicin alongside concurrent nephrotoxins and recommends agents that do not require monitoring.
children.content:
Weight-based dosing matters more in this group because lean body mass is
frequently overestimated. Review concurrent nephrotoxins before adding
gentamicin, and prefer agents that do not require monitoring.

children.title: MRSA Colonisation
children.summary: The passage details prophylaxis for MRSA colonisation, recommending teicoplanin addition to standard agents and decolonization using nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine body wash starting five days before elective surgery.
children.content:
Patients known to be colonised with meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
receive teicoplanin in addition to the standard agent for their procedure.
Decolonisation with nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine body wash should begin 5
days before elective surgery.

children.title: Audit and Compliance
children.summary: The passage details recording agent, dose, and administration time on the WHO checklist during sign-in for surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis. It specifies that compliance with a 60-minute window is audited monthly and reported to the surgical governance meeting.
children.content:
Theatre teams record the agent, dose and administration time on the WHO checklist
at the sign-in step. Compliance with the 60-minute window is audited monthly, and
results are reported to the surgical governance meeting.
